**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The copy reads as one piece.** The title "Crossing the river" and the three headings ("Early boats", "The market quay", "Going home") follow the day from dawn to the last boat. That gives a stranger the idea in one sentence and lets them predict each section before reading it. Each heading names exactly what its section holds, including the part of "The market quay" that carries over to the top of the right column (stallholders, the bench).
- **It hangs together without decoration.** It uses one serif family, near-black on white, and no rules or boxes. The quiet, plain treatment suits a calm descriptive piece about a misty morning crossing, and nothing on the page is there just to fill space. Taste: keep this restraint when revising.

**Section.** What matters first: applies. This is a text-only two-column article page with a title, three section headings and body text. I assumed the page is meant to be read straight through like an article.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The page has a clear starting point.** "Crossing the river" (about 38 px tall, bold serif, top left at roughly x 90, y 50–90) is the largest and darkest text on the page. Nothing competes with it, so the eye lands there first and then drops to "Early boats."
- **There are three levels and each is easy to tell apart.** I count three sizes and nothing in between:
  - the title, at about 38 px bold
  - the headings ("Early boats", "The market quay", "Going home"), at about 22 px bold
  - the body text, at about 17 px regular

  Each step is clearly bigger than the last. The headings also differ from the body by weight as well as size, so they stand out even at a glance across the column, which follows Refactoring UI's advice to use more than size for emphasis.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes): Arrangement and space**

- One grid: yes. There are two equal columns at x≈90 and x≈675, one gutter, and the title and headings sit on the column edges.
- Exactly aligned or clearly off: yes. The left edges are clean. The tops of the two columns (left heading ≈y121, right text ≈y118) read as level.
- Baselines across columns: **no**. Left baselines run ≈168, 193, 219… and right ≈127, 153, 178… They drift out of step after the headings, for example left 295/321 against right 288/313.
- Space inside groups smaller than between groups: yes. Headings sit closer to the text below them than to the text above.
- Boxes hold one group: yes, because there are no boxes. "The market quay" flows across the column break, which is normal for running text.
- No accidental groups: yes.
- Elements clear of each other: yes.
- Margins from the edge: yes. The left margin is about 90 px, the right about 105 px and the top about 55 px.
- Empty space gathered: yes. It is one band at the bottom (≈y520–800).
- Balance: yes. It is a top-anchored reading page, and the columns end about 67 px apart, which is normal for flowing text.
- Centering by habit: yes, since nothing is centred.
- One proportion: yes, halves.
- Eye path: yes. It runs title → left column → right column.

The entries script needs Bash, which is denied in this session. I judged the one `no` line directly.

---

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do lines of text in neighboring columns sit on the same baselines?** No. Both columns use the same body leading (≈25.5 px), but the space around the headings ("Early boats" at the top left, "The market quay" at y≈420, "Going home" at y≈251) isn't a whole number of body lines. So the two columns sit on different baselines. At the top, the right column starts at baseline ≈127 while the left starts its body at ≈168, which looks fine. Lower down they are visibly out of step: left lines at ≈295/321/346 sit beside right lines at ≈288/313/339, about 7 px off. Across the 65 px gutter the reader sees lines that almost line up but don't, so the page looks slightly unsettled rather than set. This is a convention (Bringhurst: text in neighbouring columns shares one baseline grid). The fix is to make each heading's space above plus its own line plus its space below add up to a whole number of body lines (for example, three lines of 25.5 px). Then every body line in both columns lands on the same grid. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- **Grid.** Two equal columns, one gutter, and the title and every heading hang on the column edges. The page reads as one system with no stray edges.
- **Heading spacing.** Each heading has clearly more space above it than below (≈22 px of extra space above against ≈10 px below), so it plainly belongs to the paragraph it introduces. That keeps the sections readable even though "The market quay" breaks across the columns.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (lines of text align across columns), 0 unsure

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
None.

The text holds up on every line of the checklist:
- **Size and face.** The body text is about 17–18 px in a single serif family meant for reading. Headings use the bold of that same family. The text is dark on white, well above 4.5:1.
- **Line length and spacing.** Lines run about 55–65 characters in both columns, and the line spacing suits that length.
- **Edges and breaks.** Text is set flush left. The right edge is gently uneven, with no staircase or wedge. No heading sits at the foot of a column, and no single word sits alone on a last line. The shortest last lines, "the engine." at ~x90,y320 and "the last boat." at ~x675,y440, are two or three words, which is acceptable.
- **Details.** There are no capitals in running text, no fake styles, no quotes or dashes to check, and nothing is clipped. The large title "Crossing the river" looks evenly spaced, with no gaps or collisions.

**What's working.**
- **Paragraph marks.** New paragraphs are marked with a first-line indent of about 1.5 em and no added space. The first paragraph after each heading is flush left ("The first ferry…", "The market quay is…", "In the evening…"). This follows Bringhurst's convention exactly: paragraphs read as one continuous text, and the extra space is saved for the breaks between sections.
- **Line length and spacing together.** Each line is about 60 characters with line spacing of about 1.5, so the eye finds the start of the next line easily. Short paragraphs under three plain bold subheads break the text into easy chunks.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Color: applies. The page is achromatic: near-black ink on white.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- One dark ink on a plain white ground. The headings look the same blue-black as the body and differ only by size and weight. Reading text gets the strongest possible value contrast, and the hierarchy doesn't depend on colour, so it holds in grayscale and for colour-blind readers.
- Nothing competes with the text. For a short piece of prose like this, the lack of an accent colour is the right call, not something missing.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure
